reason: The court made a case-specific S.147 discretion ruling, not a general rule that a higher court should not invite a lower court to form a contrary opinion.
The S.147 holding required a pure question of law capable of disposing of the case without evidence and going to the root of the case, not merely a jurisdiction-affecting issue.
The court held that S.147 depends on the court's opinion whether the action can be disposed of on issues of law only.
The proposition is only a vague procedural fact about adding a party and omits the statutory route and status consequences actually decided.
The court treated the absence of an order substituting the transferee as fatal to his claim to proceed as substituted plaintiff.
The court directly held that an added party could not assume the status of substituted plaintiff and file a plaint where a plaint was already before court.
The court said condominium registration was not imperative for validity, but also noted non-registration may have other legal consequences.
The case concerned non-registration of condominium property under the Apartment Ownership Law and did not establish that non-registration of any deed never affects validity.
The court required trial because the validity of Deed 854 raised mixed law and fact issues, which the extracted statement states too generally.
The substituted plaintiff remained an intestate heir because the Last Will had not been proved, a material condition omitted by the statement.
The holding was tied to deed 2078 creating a divided condominium unit and later ratification, which the broad statement drops.
The court adopted and applied the Roman-Dutch law rule that a minor's invalid contract can be ratified after majority.
The court held that after ratification on majority the contract binds the former minor as if executed after majority and operates from the original date.
The court held that a donor who reserves a right of revocation may revoke the gift by a later deed without proving reasons in court.
The validity of reserving a revocation right in a donatio propter nuptias was the sole legal issue and was decided affirmatively.
The award was set aside because denial of a hearing breached basic principles of natural justice.
The court held that a statutory tribunal deciding rights must observe natural justice even without express statutory provision.
The court expressly rejected the argument that procedural freedom allowed the tribunal to violate natural justice.
The court held that recovery of the business was distinct from recovery of the building, with occupation and materials only ancillary.
The court treated equipment, utensils, book debts and goodwill as collectable business assets of the estate.
The court held that inventory under the Civil Procedure Code follows the grant and performance of administration duties.
The statement is truncated and omits the necessary reference to proceedings under Rent Act S.22(1)(d).
The court concerned the tenant's conviction for illegal or immoral use of the premises, not any conviction of the plaintiff.
The tenancy-ending rule was limited to a conviction by a competent court for immoral or illegal use under Rent Act S.22(1)(d), not any tenant conviction.
The court adopted and applied the rule that the propounder bears the burden of proving the will of a free and capable testator.
